Improving sludge solubilization and biogas upgrading with eco-friendly 
garbage enzyme and microaerobic pretreatment: Operational parameters 
and energy balance
Somayeh Moradi a,b, Hasan Pasalari a,b, Roya Sharifi c, Mitra Gholami a,b, Mahdi Farzadkia a,b,*,  
Sami Rtimi d, Tejraj M. Aminabhavi e,f,**
a Research Center for Environmental Health Technology, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran
b Department of Environmental Health Engineering, School of Public Health, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran
c Department of Medical Laboratory Sciences, School of Allied Medical Sciences, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran
d Global Institute for Water Environment and Health, 1201, Geneva, Switzerland
e Center for Energy and Environment, School of Advanced Sciences, KLE Technological University, Hubballi, 580 031, India
f Korea University, Seoul, 02841, Republic of Korea
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Garbage enzymes
Biogas upgrading
Solubilization
Energy balance
Anaerobic digestion
Microaerobic
A B S T R A C T
A comprehensive study was performed on the effects of combined garbage enzyme (GE) fermented from orange 
peels and micro-aerobic (MA) to improve solubilization of sewage sludge (SS) and biogas production with a 
special focus on energy. The enhanced biodegradability index (sCOD) of SS was optimized under operational 
parameters including different volume ratios of GE (5, 10, and 15 % v/v), air flow rate (AFR) (0.1–0.4 VVM) and 
time (10–40 h). The effects of combined GE and MA pretreatment on the operational parameters and biomethane 
potential (BMP) was performed under mesophilic temperature (37 ± 1 ◦C) in a batch mode reactor. The results 
indicated that the highest amylase activity (80.08 U/mL), protease activity (0.94 U/mL), lipase activity (44 U/ 
mL) were achieved from the fermentation of orange peels. An increase of sCOD (2477 mg/L) was achieved in R4, 
when simultaneous GE (10 % V/V) and MA pretreatment methods were used to improve SS solubilization. The 
highest BMP (609.46 mLCH4/g VS removed) was achieved in R4, which was 1.76 fold higher than the control. 
The energy analysis indicated that the highest energy yield (85.45 kJ/g VS) was achieved in anaerobic bioreactor 
assissted with simultaneous GE and MA pretreatments. The present study is unique in the sense that it meets the 
criteria of UNSDGs Program #SGD6, #SDG7, #SDG12 and #SGD13.
1. Introduction
Over the recent years, explosive population growth led to the pro­
duction of a large amount of wastewater [1]. The treatment of waste­
water produces a huge volume of sludge and biosolids in domestic and 
industrial wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) [2]. In addition to 
harmful human and environmental effects, sludge and biosolids man­
agement account for approximately 50 % of the total cost for wastewater 
treatment [3–5]. Nowadays, a variety of physical, chemical and bio­
logical methods have been used to treat sludge in order to sludge 
reduction, sludge stabilization and value-added products [6]. It is 
important to note that physical and chemical treatment with different 
limitations including high cost and production of chemical sludge with 
high contamination hare rarely used in sludge management [7]. The 
biological processes which take advantages of low cost, high stabiliza­
tion and energy production have grasped much attention over the recent 
decades [8]. Anaerobic digestion (AD), as a biological process, is known 
as the most common technology for sludge stabilization, biogas and 
energy production [9]. AD converts organic solids present in sludge in 
the absence of oxygen into final products such as methane, carbon di­
oxide and harmless substances [10,11]. Overall, AD with four sequential 
stages (hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acteogenesis acetogenesis and meth­
anogenesis) convert the organic matter into final products [12]. Hy­
drolysis is known as the rate-limiting step in AD; the high-molecular

weight compounds are converted to smaller molecules that are 
consumed by the microorganisms [13]. A variety of different pretreat­
ment methods including physical (thermal) [14] chemical (alkalinity 
addition) [15] and biological (enzyme and micronutrient addition) [16] 
have been employed in order to accelerate the hydrolysis stage in AD, 
consequently enhancing methane and energy production [17].
The addition of hydrolytic enzyme is one of the biological pretreat­
ment methods to enhance the hydrolysis stage and biogas production 
from AD fed with recalcitrant waste and sewage sludge [18]. However, 
the main limitation imposed for the synthetic hydrolytic enzyme is the 
high cost [19]. Alternatively, the enzyme production from organic waste 
in the fermentation process, called “garbage enzyme“is considered to be 
an eco-friendly process, easy operation and low cost [20]. On the other 
hand, hydrolytic enzymes containing lipase, amylase and protease are 
easily secreted by microorganisms in the fermentation process of organic 
solid waste supplemented with carbon source (brown sugar) and 
wastewater (with consortium of microorganisms) [21]. In recent years, 
GE have grasped much attention for different environmental applica­
tions such as soil remediation, wastewater treatment, landfill leachate 
treatment and composting [22].
Negi et al., [20] examined the vermicomposting process supple­
mented with GE in order to degrade food waste along with wheat straw 
and biomass waste. The authors reported that GE led to higher quality of 
compost with higher rate of organic matter degradation (0.15 d−1) 
compared to control 0.12 d−1). Rani et al., [23] focused on lowering the 
landfill pollution index (LPI) of three landfills in Delhi, India using 
different volume ratios of GE enzyme (5, 10, 15 and 20 % (v/v)) within 
28 days. The authors used 18 parameters to calculate LPI. The authors 
reported the maximum LPI reduction of 45.47 % when 20 % volume 
ratio of GE was added to the landfill leachate (LL).
The integration of different pretreatment methods has been proposed 
for synergetic effects of hydrolysis and solubilization of organic matters 
in the AD process [24]. Micro-aerobic (MA) is a biological pretreatment 
method, involving the application of a small dose of air or oxygen 
(usually between 0.1 and 1 mg of oxygen/ l reactor per day) into an 
anaerobic system [25]. MA can improve the hydrolysis and solubiliza­
tion of organic matters as well as increasing the lipase activity. Rash­
vanlou et al. (2021) investigated the roles of MA pretreatment on sewage 
sludge solubilization and methane production in the AD process [26]. 
The results indicated that MA (volume ratio of 0.2 (vvm) and duration 
time: 40 h) led to increased sCOD from 5210 mg/L to 8580 mg/L with 
increased methane production by 221 %. In the prior literature, no 
comprehensive study has been made on the application of combined GE 
and MA for enhancing the sewage sludge solubilizationa and conse­
quently improving the methane production in AD. Therefore, the pre­
sent study was developed to investigate the roles of synergetic effects of 
GE and MA pretreatment on sludge solubilization, methane production 
and energy balance.
2. Methods and materials
2.1. Material characteristics
To investigate the effect of combined pretreatment methods (GE +
MA) on biogas production in AD, primary sludge, secondary sludge and 
inoculum samples were withdrawn from the full-scale south Tehran 
(Iran) wastewater treatment plant (STWWTP). The digested sludge as 
output of anaerobic digestion (AD) were prepared for inoculum in AD 
reactors and all biological samples were immediately transferred to the 
laboratory at 4 ◦C for further analysis. The physicochemical character­
istics of primary sludge, secondary sludge and inoculum were deter­
mined as per procedures outlined in the standard method for 
examination of water and wastewater [24]. Table 1 summarizes physi­
cochemical characteristics of primary sludge, secondary sludge and 
inoculum samples used in the study.
2.2. Production of garbage enzyme
In this study, orange fruit peels used most commonly in Iran during 
autumn and winter seasons were employed for the GE production. The 
orange peels were collected from the fruit markets and stored in a 
refrigerator at 4 ◦C for further analysis. Then, the crushed orange peels, 
brown sugar (as carbon source) and wastewater were mixed in the ratio 
of 1:3:10 (w/v) and taken in 500-mL bottles under anaerobic situation 
for fermentation process. Wastewater samples were taken from WWTP 
of food company. To ensure anaerobic condition, nitrogen gas was 
purged into different reactors for 5 min and the completely mixed 
fermentative reactors were incubated at 37 ◦C ± 1 for 21 days. After 3 
weeks of fermentation, to measure the GE produced from the fermen­
tation process, light yellowish-brown liquid supernatant were centri­
fuged at 3000 rpm for 30 min for further analysis [27].
2.3. GE (amylase, protease and lipase) measurement
2.3.1. Amylase activity
The amylase activity in GE were determined based as per Bernfeld’s 
instructions, 3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid (DNSA) method and 1 % starch as a 
substrate. Then the GE samples were centrifuged to separate superna­
tants for further analysis [28]. According to Bernfeld’s instructions, 0.5 
mL of GE sample was mixed with 0.5 mL of 1 % starch solution and 
incubated at 37 ◦C for 15 min. Next, 1 mL of DNSA colored solution was 
added to the mixture and heated to 100 ◦C for 10 min. After cooling at 
room temperature, 5 mL of distilled water was added to the produced 
solution. All steps were repeated for control sample and distilled water 
without addition of starch addition. The absorbance of different GE 
samples were recorded at 540 nm against blank using spectrophotom­
etry (Hach Company, DR-6000). Detailed information of the standard 
curve and color spectrum of different samples are provided in the sup­
porting information (see Table A.1 and Fig. A.1). Next, the amount of 
maltose released from maltose and amylase activity (U/mg) were 
calculated as:

2.3.3. Lipase activity
The lipase activity of GE was determined by the titration [30] for the 
reaction mixture containing 10 mL of pure olive live (10 % w/v), 5 mL 
arabic gum (acacia gum) (5 % w/v), 100 mL sodium hydrogen phosphate 
(0.1 M) and 100 mL distilled water that were mixed for 3 min. Next, 1 
mL of GE solution was added to the produced solution and mixed again 
at 160 rpm 35 ◦C for 15 min. Next, 20 mL ethanol (C₂H₆O) and acetone 
(C₃H₆O) were added to the mixture at a ratio of 1:1 and finally titrated 
against 0.05 M NaOH until reaching pH of 9.5;p the amount of NaOH 
consumed was considered equal to the amount of lipase activity.
2.4. MA pre-treatment process
In this study, a combined MA pretreatment was used to measure the 
effect of air flow rate (AFR) and time on enhanced sludge solubilization 
and biogas production. A 500-mL batch glass reactor with a working 
volume of 400 mL, equipped with aquarium pump (Air-pump AC 9906) 
was used to determine the role of influencing factors on sludge sCOD. On 
the other hand, the roles of different levels of AFR (air volume in sludge 
volume in 1 min (vvm)) (0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 (vvm)) and time periods 
(0, 20, 30, 40, 48, 60 h) on sCOD were investigated at 35 ◦C. Schematic 
diagram of MA reactors are presented in Fig. 1. In addition, ORP and pH 
were controlled by WTW inoLab pH 720, Xylem- WTW, Germany during 
the MA pretreatment.
2.5. Anaerobic reactors
2.5.1. Effects of different proportional ratios of GE
The experimental batch assays were performed to ascertain the cu­
mulative methane production of sludge with different volume ratios of 
GE (5 %, 10 %, and 15 %) in anaerobic reactors and controls. In total, 
four plexiglass anaerobic reactors with total and working volumes of 0.5 
and 0.4 L, placed in a mesophile incubators (37 ± 1 ◦C) were used to 
determine the effects of GE addition on BMP in anaerobic digestion 
process.
2.5.2. Effect of combined pretreatment method (MA + GE) on BMP
Considering the optimal proportional ratio of GE addition and MA, 
experimental batch assays were performed to ascertain biochemical 
methane potential (BMP) of the sludge pretreated with GE and MA in a 
separate and combined way. In total, five plexiglass anaerobic reactors 
with total and working volumes of 1 and 0.5 L, placed in a mesophilic 
incubator (37 ± 1 ◦C) were used to determine the effects of combined 
GE + MA on BMP in anaerobic digestion process. The information on 
different AD pretreated with different pretreatment methods and com­
bined pretreatment is summarized in Table 2.
To operate the AD reactors, inoculum with a constant volume ratio 
(10 %) of working volume were added to each reactor. The co-substrates 
viz., primary and excess (30:70) sludge with predefined volume ratio 
were fed to the anaerobic reactors. Prior to incubation period (24 days), 
the batch reactors were purged with pure nitrogen gas for 5 min and 
sealed with gas-tight rubber stoppers to ensure anaerobic conditions. 
The stable mesophilic temperature was maintained by circulating hot 
water and controlled by the sensor. In addition, mixing was performed 
with a mechanical stirrer with a rotational speed of 60 rpm with 5-min 
on and 1-min off throughout the experiment. The volume of methane gas 
produced by the anaerobic reactors were determined by the water 
displacement method. The schematic of laboratory installation is pre­
sented in Fig. 2. The other operational parameters including soluble 
COD (sCOD), TVFA, alkalinity, DS, VS, and pH were analyzed in the 
predefined days during the incubation period. All the measurements 
were performed in triplicate.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characterization of substrates and inoculum
Physicochemical characteristics of the primary, secondary sludge 
and inoculum samples summarized in Table 1 suggest that VS/ TS ratio 
in the primary and secondary sludge and inoculum were 75 ± 1, 82 ± 2 
and 70 ± 2, respectively. The high ratio of VS to TS in primary and 
secondary sludge indicated that organic matters in sludge samples 
facilitate the biogas production from anaerobic digestion. In addition, 
the high VS/TS for inoculum (70 %) elucidate the presence of high 
amount of potential organic matters for anaerobic digestion and biogas 
production.
3.2. GE characteristics (amylase, protease and lipase)
The specifications (sCOD and pH) of pure enzymatic solution 
extracted from the fermentation process of organic waste after 3 weeks 
were determined. The sCOD and pH of enzyme solution after the 
fermentation process were 4520 mg/L and 3.4, respectively. The enzy­
matic activity of GE solution containing amylase, protease and lipase are 
summarized in Table 3.
In addition, the values of different hydrolytic enzyme depending on 
different pH values are shown in Table 3 wherein the highest amylase 
activity (80.0894 U/mL) was determined in 5.5; the lowest amylase 
activity (78.69524 U/mL) was determined in the pH of 7.5. The reason 
for lower amount of ⍺-amylase in other pH vakues is the change in 3D 
structure of the proteins [35,36]. [27] focused on the hydrolytic activity 
of GE extracted from the mixed organic waste pineapple, orange, to­
mato, cauliflower and mango, who reported that the increased pH led to 
increased activity of the amylase in GE, which is in consistence with the 
present results. In addition, comparing the activity of organic waste in 
the study of [37] showed that the activity values of enzymes, especially 
for amylase in orange wastes were higher than those of the other wastes. 
Higher enzyme activity for the waste enzyme produced from the oranges 
could be caused by high citric acid in the composition of this fruit. 
Extracellular polymeric substances (ESP) can be degraded by citric acids 
and release of hydrolytic enzymes [37].
In addition, the protease activity in GE were determined to be 
0.940317 U/mL (see Table 3). The results indicated that the protease 
activity of this study was higher than the protease activity of the 
fermentation process of orange (0.38 U/mL) incubated in 90 days [27]. 
The most possible reasons for higher protease activity in the present 
study are attributed to higher operational temperature (35 ◦C) and mi­
crobial active area due to little size of orange peels. The lipase enzyme, 
which was measured by titration in pH 9.5 was calculated to be 44 mL. 
Rahman et al., [38] used the vegetable waste during the fermentation 
time of 30 days to extract the waste enzymes. The maximum activity of 
amylase, protease and lipase were measured to be 1.782 U/mg, 0.050 U/ 
mg and 0.355 U/mg, respectively under the optimal conditions. Notice 
that these values are lower than the values measured in the present 
study.
3.3. Pretreatment processes
3.3.1. The effects of GE addition on biogas production
Table A.3 shows the effects of GE addition with different volumetric 
ratios (5, 10, and 15 %) on biogas production in anaerobic reactors. It is 
observed that the highest cumulative methane production (8100 mL) 
was in the reactor pretreated with 10 % GE, followed by 5 % (7095 mL) 
and 15 % (6900 mL), respectively. In addition, there are significant 
differences between the methane production in different reactors pre­
treated with GE and control (p-value<0.05). Nazim et al., [39] investi­
gated the treatment of gray water using different proportional volume 
ratios of GE (5, 10, 20, 50 %); these results showed that 10 % (V/V) of GE 
was the optimum condition for the removal of TDS (58 %), BOD5 (65 %) 
and COD (79 %). The further increased volume ratio of GE increases the 
activity of enzymes and lower the pH, which suppresses the activity of 
the enzymes.
3.3.2. Effects of MA pretreatment on sludge solubility
MA pretreatment method was used to enhance the biodegradability 
index of the sludge before feeding into the AD process and biogas pro­
duction. To this end, the effects of influencing parameters including AFR

and time on sCOD was determined as shown in Fig. 3, which indicate the 
variation of sCOD as a function of AFR and time. As shown in Fig. 3(a), 
there is a two-stage trend for sCOD of sludge by increasing the AFR; the 
sCOD increased from 2450 mg/L to 4045 mg/L when the AFR increased 
from 0 in control sample to 0.2 vvm. However, the decreasing trend was 
observed by further increasing the AFR. Therefore, AFR equal to 0.2 vvm 
was considered optimum AFR with the highest sCOD.
In the case of time, there is a similar and two-step trend for sCOD of 
sludge (see Fig. 3 (b)). As shown in Fig. 3(b), the sCOD increased from 
2450 mg/L to 3724 mg/L, when the time increased from 0 to 40 h. 
Therefore, the MA time equal to 40 h was considered as the optimum 
condition. The MA pretreatment increased the biodegradability and 
hydrolysis of the complex organic matters via providing suitable con­
ditions for the growth of hydrolytic microorganisms and accordingly, 
the hydrolytic enzymes including the lipase [40,41]. Montalvo et al., 
[42] reported that the highest solubility of sewage sludge (PS: WAS: 40: 
60) by the MA was achieved at 48 h of aeration and AFR equal to 0.3 
vvm, which are comparable with the results presented here.
3.4. Anaerobic digestion performance
3.4.1. Biogas upgrading
The performance of anaerobic reactors in terms of daily biogas 
production and cumulative biogas production during the 24-day incu­
bation period is presented in Fig. 4(a-b). The cumulative methane pro­
duction from different reactors pretreated with separate, combined 
methods and control are presented in Fig. 4(a). As indicated in Fig. 4(a), 
the highest cumulative methane production was observed in R4 (9855 
mL), where simultaneous MA and GE was performed for the pretreat­
ment method, followed by R3 (9345 mL) with combined MA and GE 
pretreatment methods. Notice that R2 with MA pretreatment method 
and R1, as control produced 6105 mL and 5405 mL, respectively within 
the 24-day incubation period. These methane production analysis 
confirm that the simultaneous MA and GE pretreatment methods 
experienced synergetic effects on biodegradability of organic matters in 
anaerobic digestion, consequently increasing further the methane pro­
duction. On the other hand, the simultaneous MA and GE increased 
more sCOD, as the biodegradability of sludge, thereby providing more 
substrate for methanogenic bacteria in order to produce more methane 
in the anaerobic digestion [43].
Fig. 4(b) shows the daily methane production in different anaerobic 
reactors, wherein similar trends are observed in different anaerobic re­
actors pretreated with different methods within the incubation period; 
the methane production increased from the initial days of the operation 
that gradually decreased until the end of the incubation period of 
anaerobic digestion. The highest methane production was observed in

Table 4 summarizes detailed information on the BMP of different 
anaerobic reactors assisted with different pretreatment methods, where 
the highest BMP (609.46 mLCH4/g VS removed) was observed in R4, in 
which the simultaneous GE and MA were employed to solubilize the 
sewage sludge, followed by R3 (580.07 mLCH4/g VS) and R2 (390.09

GE and MA enhanced the BMP by 1.76 fold compared to the control. 
Zhang et al., [44] investigated the effects of microwave pretreatment 
(MW) on biogas upgrading of anaerobic reactor fed with food waste 
(FW) and sewage sludge (SS). The authors reported that the highest BMP 
(338.44 mL CH4/ g VSadded) when the optimal ratio of FW:SS (3:2) was 
fed to the mesophilica anaerobic reactors. Cherukuri et al., [45] focused 
on the improvement of the biogas production from anaerobic digestion 
of FW using the thermal pretreatment under mesophilic temperature. 
The highest BMP (730 mL/g VSfed) was achieved, which is comparable 
with the results of this study.
3.4.2. The sCOD variation and VS reduction (VSR) in anaerobic reactors
Fig. 5 shows the sCOD variations in different anaerobic digestion 
reactors, where a similar two-step trends for sCOD were observed in 
different anaerobic reactors during the incubation period. The sCOD 
increased during the fisrt and lag phase of anaerobic digestion, which 
gradually decreased due to the consumption of methanogenic bacteria 
as the substrates [46]. In addition, the highest increased sCOD concen­
tration was observed in R4 (the difference between day 5 and day 1, was 
2447 mg/ L), followed by R 3 (1773), R2 (270), and R1 (270). The 
simultaneous GE and MA pretreatments were able to effectively disin­
tegrate the biological solids of the sludge to provide more soluble mat­
ters for microorganisms [47]. Arun et al., [18] focused on the synergic 
effects of ultrasound and GE on the waste activated sludge (WAS) of the 
dairy industry. The results showed that the addition of 35 mL of GE to 
50 mL of WAS of dairy products experienced the greatest decrease in SS, 
sCOD, soluble protein, carbohydrates 27.45 %, 28.36 %, 987 mg/ L and 
932 mg /L, respectively. Furthermore, at the end of the incubation 
period, the remaining sCOD in R4 and R3 were observed to be between 
4200 and 4300 mg/L, while the remaining sCOD for R2 (pretreated by 
MA) and control were and 1200 and 1110 mg/L, respectively.
The VSR for different anaerobic reactors within the incubation 
period are summarized in Table 5, where the highest VSR was observed 
in R3 (52.07 %); here, the combined GE + MA was used to enhance the 
methane production followed by R4 (49.02 %) and R2 (41.45 %).
3.4.3. pH and total volatile fatty acids (TVFA) variations in anaerobic 
reactors
The pH variation of different anaerobic reactors illustrated in Fig. 6
(a), suggest the same trend of pH for different anaerobic reactors; the pH 
showed decreasing trend in initial and hydrolysis stages of the anaerobic 
digestion that gradually increased when the methanogenic bacteria 
consumed TVFA for methane production [48]. The lowest pH was 
observed in R4 (5.9), where simultaneous GE and MA were used for 
enhanced methane production. The higher TVFA in R4 and R3 are the 
main possible reasons for lower pH in initial stages of the anaerobic 
digestion compared to other reactors. In addition, the same trend of pH 
variations were observed in different studies focused on the improve­
ment of biogas production with pretreatment methods [49,50].
The TVFA variations in different anaerobic reactors illustrated in 
Fig. 6(b) shows that TVFA in different reactors increased during the first 
phase of anaerobic reactors, which gradually decreased due to the 
consumption of TVFA for methane production by the methanogenic 
bacteria. The highest TVFA was observed in R4 (6050 mg/L) followed by 
R3 (5120 mg/L). The results indicate that simultaneous pretreatment 
methods (GE + MA) significantly increased the TVFA needed for 
methanogenic bacteria in order to produce more of methane [51,52]. Lu 
et al., [53] surveyed the VFA production from the potato peel waste. The 
authors examined the effects of different pH levels (5, 7, 11) on the 
concentration and composition of VFA, intermediate products and 
metabolic status, showed the highest TVFA, suggesting that the highest 
concentration of total VFA was 41.9 mg COD/L obtained at pH 7.0.
3.5. Potential energy recovery from anaerobic co-digestion
Table 6 summaries the energy balance including energy production 
and energy consumption (electricity and heat) for different anaerobic 
reactors assisted with different pretreatment processes. The output en­
ergy obtained from the anaerobic reactors were estimated to and found 
to be between 108.36 and 193.70 kJ/g VSremoved; the highest value 
was for R4 (193.70 kJ/g VSremoved), followed by R3 (184.15 kJ/g 
VSremoved). Therefore, the energy yield in pretreated anaerobic re­
actors with MA combined and simultaneous pretreatment experienced 
increases of 14.51 kJ/g VS, 75.71 kJ/g VS and 85.45 kJ/g VS compared 
to control reactors without the pretreatment process.
Additionally, the total energy balance, difference between the energy 
yield and energy consumption by different anaerobic reactors indicated 
that there is a significant difference between the energy balance for 
reactors assisted with pretreatment methods and control; the highest 
energy balance observed was for R4 (193.70 kJ/g VS). This differences 
was estimated to be 85.34 kJ/g VS compared to the control (108.36 kJ/g 
VS). Liu et al., [54] studied the effect of microwave (MW) pretreatment 
on the anaerobic digestion of sludge (SS) and food waste (FW). The re­
sults obtained showed the highest net energy output achieved using the 
MW pretreatment that were 76.25 kJ/g Fed VS.

bioavailability for enhanced methane and energy production using eco- 
friendly and economic pretreatment method. The GE fermented from GE 
and MA were utilized to enhance the energy production from SS. It was 
found that simultaneous GE and MA is a feasible promising technology 
to enhance methane and energy production from the SS under meso­
philic temperature. The highest BMP (609.46 mLCH4/g VS removed) 
were achieved in R4, where the simultaneous GE and MA were utilized 
under the optimal conditions. The highest cumulative methane pro­
duction (9855 mL) was observed in R4, which was 1.82 folds higher than 
the control (5405 mL). The energy balance analysis indicated a signifi­
cant difference between the highest energy yield (+193.70 kJ/g VS) and 
the energy produced from the control (+108.36 kJ/g VS). Therefore, the 
SS anaerobic reactor can be considered as the promising and cost- 
effective method. Further research is recommended to investigate the 
methane content and methanogenic pathway occurring by the pre­
dominant microorganisms. The present study meets the required criteria
